title: AI Interpretation for TB, HIV, and Hepatitis Care
summary: AI medical interpretation supports infectious disease clinics with accurate TB, HIV, and hepatitis communication this October 2026.
body_markdown:
###


Opalite Health covers 150+ languages for real-time AI interpretation, NoBarrier supports roughly 45 through AI, and Lexi supports about 35+. For TB, HIV, and hepatitis programs that need broad coverage across rooms, telehealth, and phone, Opalite is one of the widest AI-native options currently available for infectious disease workflows.


###


An AI medical interpreter delivers real-time, two-way spoken interpretation during a clinical encounter, tracking terminology, negations, and medication details across languages. Google Translate is a general consumer tool without medical terminology optimization, healthcare workflow integration, encounter documentation, or the privacy controls a clinic needs for TB, HIV, or hepatitis care.


###


Yes. Start with a 6 to 8 week pilot covering TB intake, HIV new diagnosis, and hepatitis testing, then use Opalite for scheduling, medication counseling, and follow-ups while keeping LanguageLine available for patient preference or escalation. Document teach-back results, language use, and any escalations to measure fit before expanding.


###


Ask the patient to restate the difference in plain language: HCV cure means an undetectable RNA result 12 weeks after therapy ends, while HBV requires ongoing monitoring. Lock that distinction with a teach-back before the visit closes, and send a translated take-home sheet that names the lab, the timing, and who calls with results.


###


Allow outbound UDP ports 3478 and 50000 to 60000 for WebRTC audio, test microphones at multiple distances with masks and HVAC noise present, and configure SSO with role-based access and retention settings that match your privacy policy. Set a fallback path, such as push-to-talk or phone interpretation, before go-live so any connectivity gap does not interrupt a sensitive HIV or TB conversation.


###


Offer a human interpreter when a patient asks for one, when clinic policy calls for it, or when the AI system flags low confidence in a conversation. Human interpreters also make sense if comprehension problems persist after teach-back, even with careful read-backs and plain language. None of this stems from a legal mandate tied to TB, HIV, or hepatitis visits specifically. Instead, treat human interpretation as one option within a broader language-access program, chosen based on patient preference and clinical judgment.
